clinicalPearls: A congenital myopathy with a wide severity spectrum, from a severe neonatal form with profound hypotonia and respiratory failure to milder childhood and adult-onset forms
Weakness is typically most marked in facial, bulbar, neck-flexor and proximal limb muscles, and a long thin face with a high-arched palate is characteristic
Caused by variants in several sarcomeric thin-filament genes, most commonly nebulin (NEB, usually recessive) and skeletal actin (ACTA1), with tropomyosin and troponin genes also implicated

Muscle biopsy hallmark is nemaline rods (thread-like bodies) within fibres, best seen as red-purple inclusions on the modified Gomori trichrome stain and confirmed on electron microscopy as electron-dense structures arising from the Z-disc
Respiratory muscle weakness may be disproportionate to limb weakness and can occur even when limb strength is relatively preserved
Creatine kinase is usually normal or mildly elevated
Cardiac involvement is uncommon but has been described, so periodic cardiac review is reasonable in more severe cases
reference.pathophysiology: Nemaline myopathy is a congenital myopathy caused by variants in genes encoding thin-filament and Z-disc-associated proteins of the skeletal muscle sarcomere, including nebulin, skeletal alpha-actin, and the tropomyosin and troponin genes. Disruption of thin-filament assembly and regulation impairs force generation and leads to the aggregation of Z-disc material into the characteristic rod-like inclusions. The resulting contractile dysfunction produces predominantly proximal, facial and bulbar weakness with notable respiratory muscle involvement. Inheritance may be autosomal recessive or dominant depending on the causative gene.
additionalInvestigations: Muscle biopsy with Gomori trichrome staining and electron microscopy to demonstrate nemaline rods
Genetic panel testing covering NEB, ACTA1, TPM2, TPM3, TNNT1 and related genes
Respiratory function testing including assessment for nocturnal hypoventilation
Swallowing and nutritional assessment in infants and severely affected patients
Electromyography to confirm a myopathic pattern and exclude neuropathic causes
redFlags: Neonatal respiratory failure or apnoea requiring ventilatory support
Progressive nocturnal hypoventilation with morning headaches or daytime somnolence
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends strongly on subtype: the severe neonatal form carries a high risk of early respiratory failure, whereas typical congenital and milder forms are often static or slowly progressive and compatible with prolonged survival and useful function. Respiratory surveillance is the key determinant of long-term outcome.
pitfalls: Underestimating respiratory muscle weakness because limb strength appears adequate
Missing rods because trichrome staining or electron microscopy was not performed
Confusing the myopathic facial and bulbar weakness with a neuromuscular junction disorder
Assuming a normal creatine kinase excludes a congenital myopathy
